Key Finding: Mobile agricultural information services raise recommended practice adoption and yields among smallholders when tailored to local farming contexts, though low literacy and connectivity still constrain reach.
APA Reference: Fabregas, R., Kremer, M., & Schilbach, F. (2019). Realizing the potential of digital development: The case of agricultural advice. Science, 366(6471), eaay3038. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aay3038

Key Finding: Agricultural mobile initiatives frequently underperform when designed without local user participation, low-literacy interfaces, or sustained institutional integration beyond short pilot phases.
APA Reference: Aker, J. C., Ghosh, I., & Burrell, J. (2016). The promise (and pitfalls) of ICT for agriculture initiatives. Agricultural Economics, 47(S1), 35-48. https://doi.org/10.1111/agec.12301

Key Finding: Smallholder uptake of mobile agricultural services remains uneven because usability barriers, fragmented content, and weak trust limit routine field use despite rapid mobile phone proliferation.
APA Reference: Baumüller, H. (2018). The little we know: An exploratory literature review on the utility of mobile phone-enabled services for smallholder farmers. Journal of International Development, 30(1), 134-154. https://doi.org/10.1002/jid.3314

Key Finding: Open-source Android phenotyping apps that pair offline trait capture with barcode scanning substantially reduce transcription errors and post-harvest data preparation time compared with paper field sheets.
APA Reference: Rife, T. W., & Poland, J. A. (2014). Field Book: An open-source application for field data collection on Android. Crop Science, 54(4), 1624-1627. https://doi.org/10.2135/cropsci2013.08.0579

Key Finding: Standardized numeric coding of cassava foliage, stem, and storage root descriptors enables consistent germplasm characterization and cross-site statistical comparison across research programs.
APA Reference: Fukuda, W. M. G., Guevara, C. L., Kawuki, R., & Ferguson, M. E. (2010). Selected morphological and agronomic descriptors for the characterization of cassava. IITA. https://doi.org/10.25502/pfbm-9233/p

Key Finding: Harmonized plant-part descriptor lists with fixed categorical scales allow taro characterization datasets collected across dispersed field sites to be exchanged and analyzed without manual recoding.
APA Reference: International Plant Genetic Resources Institute. (1999). Descriptors for taro (Colocasia esculenta). IPGRI. https://hdl.handle.net/10568/73039

Key Finding: Root and tuber crops generate major caloric and income value for developing-country smallholders, yet underinvestment in seed systems and trait evaluation restricts productivity gains and market expansion.
APA Reference: Scott, G. J. (2021). A review of root, tuber and banana crops in developing countries: Past, present and future. International Journal of Food Science & Technology, 56(3), 1093-1114. https://doi.org/10.1111/ijfs.14778

Key Finding: Cassava, sweet potato, yams, and aroids underpin low-input rural livelihoods across tropical regions, making reliable cultivar characterization essential for improving farm yields and processing value.
APA Reference: Lebot, V. (2020). Tropical root and tuber crops: Cassava, sweet potato, yams and aroids (2nd ed.). CABI. https://doi.org/10.1079/9781789243369.0000

Key Finding: Global surveys of developing-country sweetpotato researchers rank varietal selection for yield, pest resistance, and postharvest quality among the highest-return investments for smallholder farm income.
APA Reference: Fuglie, K. O. (2007). Priorities for sweetpotato research in developing countries: Results of a survey. HortScience, 42(5), 1200-1206. https://doi.org/10.21273/HORTSCI.42.5.1200

Key Finding: Cassava maintains stable or improved suitability under projected climate warming relative to major cereals, highlighting the value of characterizing resilient cultivars across diverse agro-ecological zones.
APA Reference: Jarvis, A., Ramirez-Villegas, J., Herrera Campo, B. V., & Navarro-Racines, C. (2012). Is cassava the answer to African climate change adaptation? Tropical Plant Biology, 5(1), 9-29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12042-012-9096-7

Key Finding: Cassava tolerates drought, high temperatures, and marginal soils better than staple grains, positioning trait-documented root crops as vital buffers for food security under intensifying climate shocks.
APA Reference: Pushpalatha, R., & Gangadharan, B. (2020). Is cassava (Manihot esculenta Crantz) a climate smart crop? A review in the context of bridging future food demand gap. Tropical Plant Biology, 13(3), 201-211. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12042-020-09255-2

Key Finding: Global agricultural research remains heavily skewed toward major cereals while climate-resilient root and tuber crops receive disproportionately little research attention relative to future climate needs.
APA Reference: Manners, R., & van Etten, J. (2018). Are agricultural researchers working on the right crops to enable food and nutrition security under future climates? Global Environmental Change, 53, 182-194. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2018.09.010

Key Finding: The International Treaty obligates contracting parties to conserve, characterize, and share plant genetic resources sustainably while recognizing farmers rights over traditional crop varieties.
APA Reference: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. (2009). International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture. https://www.fao.org/faolex/results/details/en/c/LEX-FAOC033161/

Key Finding: National Philippine policy formally mandates dedicated root crop research, varietal improvement, and training centers at Visayas State University and Benguet State University to strengthen root crop systems.
APA Reference: Republic of the Philippines. (1977). Presidential Decree No. 1107: Establishing the Philippine Root Crops Research and Training Center. https://www.chanrobles.com/presidentialdecrees/presidentialdecreeno1107.html

Key Finding: Global agrobiodiversity assessments warn that genetic erosion of local crop varieties is accelerating due to weak national monitoring systems and fragmented characterization data across public institutions.
APA Reference: Bélanger, J., & Pilling, D. (Eds.). (2019). The state of the world's biodiversity for food and agriculture. FAO. https://doi.org/10.4060/CA3129EN

Key Finding: Philippine law mandates transparency, legitimate purpose, proportionality, and informed consent whenever personal information is collected, processed, or shared by digital platforms.
APA Reference: Republic of the Philippines. (2012). Republic Act No. 10173: Data Privacy Act of 2012. Official Gazette. https://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/2012/08/15/republic-act-no-10173/

Key Finding: Implementing regulations require data controllers to enforce strict retention limits, purpose limitation, security safeguards, and data subject rights including access, correction, and erasure.
APA Reference: National Privacy Commission. (2016). Implementing Rules and Regulations of Republic Act No. 10173. https://privacy.gov.ph/implementing-rules-and-regulations-ra-10173/

Key Finding: Access and benefit-sharing law requires prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms when genetic resources or associated traditional knowledge are accessed and shared across jurisdictions.
APA Reference: Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity. (2011). Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from their Utilization. https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/nagoya-protocol-en.pdf

Key Finding: Asymmetric control over agricultural datasets lets large platforms capture commercial value from grower-generated field records while exposing farmers to privacy loss and unfair market leverage.
APA Reference: Carbonell, I. M. (2016). The ethics of big data in big agriculture. Internet Policy Review, 5(1), 1-13. https://doi.org/10.14763/2016.1.405

Key Finding: Agricultural data platforms embed ethical and power choices in how data are collected and shared, risking smallholder marginalization unless transparency and community benefit govern platform design.
APA Reference: Bronson, K., & Knezevic, I. (2016). Big Data in food and agriculture. Big Data & Society, 3(1), 1-5. https://doi.org/10.1177/2053951716648174

Key Finding: Digital farming platforms can extract high-resolution spatial and agronomic field data in ways that erode farmer autonomy unless governance protects data sovereignty and limits exploitative reuse.
APA Reference: Fraser, A. (2019). Land grab/data grab: Precision agriculture and its new horizons. The Journal of Peasant Studies, 46(5), 893-912. https://doi.org/10.1080/03066150.2017.1415887
